sysd-found-143.title: Software architecture erosion: when the build drifts from the plan
sysd-found-143.text: Between the architecture a team intends and the one it builds, a gap tends to open. Software architecture erosion is that gradual gap, widening over time between a system's intended and implemented architecture. Its causes are architectural violations, accumulating technical debt and knowledge vaporization, and it can decrease performance, substantially increase evolutionary costs and degrade software quality. Enforcing architectural rules, regular code reviews and automated testing help prevent it. Refactoring, redesign and documentation updates remedy it, and conformance checks and static analysis detect it early. When documentation is out of date or the architecture has eroded, architecture recovery uncovers the architecture from the implementation and documentation.

sysd-found-144.title: Requirements engineering: settling the what before the how
sysd-found-144.text: Before anyone designs a solution, someone has to settle what the system must do. Requirements engineering is the work of eliciting, analysing, specifying, validating and managing what a system must do, the 'what' that architecture answers with a 'how'. It addresses the problem space, while software architecture, covered in {{ref:sysd-found-138}}, targets the solution space. The waterfall model makes it the first phase of development. Later methods such as the Rational Unified Process assume it continues through a system's lifetime. Required behavior impacts the solution architecture, which may introduce new requirements in turn, and the Twin Peaks model aims to exploit this relation.

sysd-found-208.title: Software design pattern: a template for a recurring problem
sysd-found-208.text: Some problems come up so often in code that their solutions have names. A software design pattern is a reusable template for solving a commonly needed behavior in software. It is a template for a type of problem, not a rigid structure to copy into source code. It works below architecture patterns, which solve broader challenges. Reusing proven patterns speeds up development and helps prevent subtle issues. Patterns are grouped as creational, structural, behavioral and concurrency patterns. Critics say a need for a pattern may signal a missing language feature. Of the 23 patterns in Design Patterns, 16 are simplified or eliminated in Lisp or Dylan.

sysd-found-140.title: Architectural patterns and styles: the vocabulary of structure
sysd-found-140.text: The vocabulary for the shape of a system is crowded, and its edges blur. A software architecture pattern is a reusable, proven solution to a recurring system-level problem about overall structure, component interactions and quality attributes. It sits at a higher level of abstraction than a software design pattern, covered in {{ref:sysd-found-208}}. An architecture style is a high-level structural organization. It says how components are organized, how they interact and what constrains those interactions, using a vocabulary of component and connector types. Styles are the most coarse-grained level of system organization, for example layered architecture and hexagonal architecture, besides those covered in {{ref:sysd-msg-083}} and {{ref:sysd-msg-020}}.

sysd-found-133.title: Requirements clarification: ask before you design
sysd-found-133.text: The first move with a vague interview question is to ask questions back. Requirements clarification means asking early about the exact scope of the problem and sorting what the system must do into functional, non-functional and extended requirements. Functional requirements are the basic functionalities the end user demands, all of which must be built into the system as part of the contract. Ask which features to design for and which edge cases to consider. Non-functional requirements are quality constraints, so ask about aspects such as data volume, availability and scale. For example, every request should be handled with minimum delay, and the system should be highly available. Extended requirements are nice-to-have items that may be out of scope, such as recording metrics and analytics or tracking the health and performance of the service.

sysd-found-132.title: The system design interview framework, step by step
sysd-found-132.text: A system design question is open-ended, but a good answer follows a fixed order. The order is to clarify requirements, estimate capacity, design the high-level structure, the data and the interfaces, then address scale and reliability. Start by clarifying requirements, covered in {{ref:sysd-found-133}}. Ask about the core features and about aspects such as data volume, availability and scale. Estimate capacity next, meaning the number of users, traffic, storage and memory needs, and compute and networking requirements. Useful questions are the desired scale, the read/write ratio, requests per second and storage needed. Define the data model early. List the entities and the relationships between them, which shows the data flow at the core of every system. Then choose a type of data store and settle the schema. Design the APIs as a simple interface of parameters, functions, classes, types and entities, without writing code. Keep it simple and revisit it when covering extended requirements. Then break the system into components such as client apps, servers, load balancers and data stores. Draw a simple block diagram, focus on the data flow, and walk through how the system works from the client's perspective. In the detailed design, pick with the interviewer the major components to go deeper on. Examples are data partitioning, load distribution, a cache and handling a sudden traffic spike. Finish with bottlenecks and reliability. Ask whether there are enough replicas of the data and whether any part's failure would stop everything. Ask whether the data needs sharding, and how to make the system and its cache more robust.

sysd-found-135.title: Machine learning systems design: a model inside a system
sysd-found-135.text: Recommendation engines, fraud detection and natural language processing all depend on systems built around a machine learning model. Machine learning systems design builds scalable, reliable and efficient systems that integrate machine learning models to solve real-world problems. The key components are problem definition, which covers data requirements and evaluation metrics, and a data pipeline. The others are model selection and training, deployment and serving, and watching and maintaining the running system. The design balances trade-offs between accuracy, response delay, cost and maintainability. It overlaps with MLOps, practices that unify machine learning development and operations to ease deployment and lifecycle management.

sysd-found-209.title: Conway's law: software mirrors the organization
sysd-found-209.text: Software tends to look like the organization that wrote it. Conway's law says that the structure of a system mirrors the communication structure of the organization that designs it. The reason is that the authors of a product's parts must communicate to keep them compatible, so the technical structure reflects the organization's social boundaries. Strictly, the law describes a correspondence, not a cause, and commentators differ on whether design drives the organization, the organization drives design, or both. Researchers at MIT and Harvard Business School found strong evidence for it. The product from the loosely-coupled organization was significantly more modular than the product from the tightly-coupled one.

sysd-found-134.title: Discussing trade-offs in an interview without preaching
sysd-found-134.text: A blanket claim that one kind of data store is simply better and another does not scale reflects poorly in an interview. In the detailed design stage, present different approaches with their advantages and disadvantages, and explain design decisions with examples. This is a good time to show expertise, but avoid being too opinionated about technologies. Singh advises being humble about what you know and do not know, and using existing knowledge with examples to navigate this part of the interview. The framework this stage belongs to is described in {{ref:sysd-found-132}}.

openers.what-system-design-is-and-how-interviews: System design is the process of defining the architecture, interfaces and data of a system so that it satisfies specific requirements. This chapter introduces the field, the interview built around it, and the vocabulary of requirements and architecture that the rest of the course leans on. A functional requirement says what a system is supposed to accomplish, a non-functional one says how it should operate, and software architecture is the set of structures needed to reason about both. The interview that tests all of this has no single expected answer.
openers.found: Before anyone draws a box on a whiteboard, a design needs requirements to satisfy. This part gives you the language to work from them: what system design is, how an interview tests it, and the standard components, six broad categories of them, that designs are assembled from. It separates the behavior a system is supposed to accomplish from the overall properties, such as availability or performance, by which its operation is judged. Along the way come eight problems that recur in large-scale production systems, each with a standard remedy, and the practices that keep an architecture honest as it evolves.

reviews.what-system-design-is-and-how-interviews: System design defines a system's architecture, interfaces and data so that it satisfies its requirements, and the interview that tests it has no single expected answer. Functional requirements say what the system is supposed to accomplish, non-functional ones say how it is supposed to be, and requirements engineering is the work of finding and managing both before architecture answers with a how. Architecture is the set of structures a team reasons with, and decision records, four core activities and watchfulness about erosion keep it honest as the system evolves. In the interview these ideas become a sequence, from clarifying requirements and estimating capacity to addressing scale and reliability, with trade-offs presented humbly along the way.
